content: 1. A solid orange bar of 3HR is provided to last until the child’s 3-month clinic visit. At this visit, the child is assessed and documented to have completed tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT). 2. Health emergencies, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, have disrupted the delivery of health services. This disruption can occur directly due to the focus on the emergency or indirectly due to measures implemented to control the emergency. 3. The COVID-19 pandemic has reversed years of progress in providing essential tuberculosis (TB) services and reducing the disease burden. There has been a significant global decline in the number of newly diagnosed and reported TB cases, with 8 million cases reported in 2020, a level last seen in 2012. 4. Reduced access to TB diagnosis and treatment has led to an increase in TB-related deaths, with the number of deaths in 2020 returning to 2017 levels. 5. Programmatic support for TB care includes adherence support and screening for TB and adverse events, which should be provided at least monthly. This support can be delivered virtually, in the community, or through a combination of these methods to maintain differentiated service delivery (DSD) models and reduce contact with health facilities. 6. HIV-negative children aged 2 years and older can receive 3HP, but 3HR is currently the most suitable TPT regimen due to the availability of child-friendly fixed-dose combination (FDC) HR 50/75 mg and the lack of a child-friendly formulation of rifapentine. 7. Children and young adolescents have been disproportionately affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, with TB notifications in children under 5 years decreasing by 28% and in children aged 5–14 years by 21% between 2019 and 2020, compared to an 18% decrease in people aged 15 years and older. 8. Vulnerable groups, such as children and adolescents, are more likely to experience negative impacts from health emergencies due to their dependence on adults for accessing healthcare. Indirect impacts, such as reduced household income, increased poverty, food insecurity, malnutrition, missed health checks, missed vaccinations, and missed schooling, may also influence TB outcomes. 9. National TB programs (NTPs) should ensure that children and adolescents are not left behind when designing and implementing innovative approaches to maintain TB service delivery during health emergencies and recovery stages. 10. In May 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) updated its guidance on TB considerations in the context of COVID-19 to help countries maintain continuity of TB services. These approaches should be people-centered and leverage opportunities across both diseases, such as simultaneous testing for respiratory symptoms to minimize missed diagnoses and provide appropriate management. 11. Invasive sample collection procedures, such as sputum induction, increase the risk of TB and COVID-19 transmission if infection control measures are not followed. Less invasive sample collection methods should be prioritized in such scenarios. 12. NTPs should ensure uninterrupted supplies of child-friendly formulations and provide adequate refills to enhance treatment completion and minimize frequent trips to health facilities. This can be achieved through multi-month dispensing or community delivery of TB medicines. 13. Efforts should be made to ensure neonatal and infant Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination continues without interruption. 14. Integrated, patient-centered care and prevention are key pillars of the End TB Strategy. The roadmap to ending TB in children and adolescents emphasizes the importance of integrated familyand community-centered strategies for TB care. 15. Decentralized, integrated, family-centered models of TB care have been recommended for TB case detection and provision of TPT. Case studies demonstrate that these approaches can improve pediatric TB case detection and TPT uptake. 16. Planning for decentralized, integrated, patientand family-centered services should include policy analysis, stakeholder analysis, human resources capacity assessment, resource mapping, access to TB medicines (including child-friendly formulations), health information management, and health service delivery mapping. 17. Enhanced engagement of the private sector in child and adolescent TB services is crucial to ensure access to necessary TB services for all children and adolescents. 18. Differentiated service delivery (DSD) as a people-centered approach to health service delivery can be applied to children and adolescents with TB or at risk of TB. 19. Health emergencies that disrupt the delivery of or access to health services can have direct and indirect negative impacts on child and adolescent TB services. Innovative approaches to mitigate these impacts should consider the specific needs of children and adolescents with TB or exposed to TB. 20. Children and adolescents living with HIV are at increased risk of TB exposure, infection, progression to disease, and TB-related morbidity and mortality. This risk is influenced by the degree of immune suppression. 21. Childhood HIV infection is particularly common in settings with high antenatal HIV prevalence and limited implementation of interventions to prevent vertical transmission. In these settings, HIV prevalence is high among infants and young children, who are also at risk for TB. 22. In TBand HIV-endemic regions, TB is common in children living with HIV, and HIV infection is common in children with TB. Routine HIV testing is recommended for all children and adolescents with presumed or diagnosed TB. 23. In 2020, of the 226,000 TB-related deaths in children, 21,000 (9%) occurred in children living with HIV. Among 210,000 children notified with TB in 16 high TB/HIV burden countries, 68% had an HIV test result recorded, and 86% of those with TB/HIV co-infection were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). 24. Children under 10 years living with HIV should be screened for TB at every healthcare encounter using a symptom screen that includes cough, fever, poor weight gain, or close contact with a person with TB. 25. The WHO-recommended W4SS (current cough, fever, weight loss, and night sweats) is a simple, non-invasive screening tool that can be implemented in any setting. However, its results are subjective and depend on the patient’s understanding and willingness to report symptoms, as well as the provider’s interpretation. 26. W4SS has relatively high sensitivity (83%) but low specificity (38%) in adults and adolescents living with HIV. Among outpatients on ART, its sensitivity is lower (53%), indicating that W4SS alone is insufficient for TB detection in people receiving regular ART care. 27. Despite its limitations, W4SS is an essential part of clinical examination and the most accessible screening tool at all levels of the health system. It can be repeated as needed, with more intensive screening strategies used less frequently. 28. C-reactive protein (CRP), an indicator of systemic inflammation, can be measured with a simple, affordable, and feasible point-of-care fingerprick test. Results are available within 3–5 minutes, enabling quick clinical decisions for TB diagnostic evaluation or TPT initiation. 29. Sequential use of a positive W4SS followed by CRP testing with a cut-off of >5 mg/L is supported for TB screening, particularly in people not on ART. CRP can also help rule out TB disease before initiating TPT. 30. Chest X-ray (CXR) is useful for TB screening in people living with HIV and is recommended by WHO alongside W4SS for ruling out TB disease before starting TPT. A positive or abnormal result on either CXR or W4SS indicates the need for further diagnostic evaluation. 31. Children and adolescents living with HIV should not receive BCG vaccination due to the risk of disseminated BCG disease. However, those on ART who are clinically well and immunologically stable may be vaccinated. 32. Children and adolescents living with HIV who are household contacts of people with infectious TB should be evaluated for TB disease and either treated for TB or given TPT if screening suggests they are unlikely to have TB disease. 33. Adolescents and children aged 12 months and older living with HIV who are unlikely to have TB disease should receive TPT as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of TB contact history.
